 High spirits, Election Day fervor kept hundreds of students waiting in line for hours at UC Merced vote center 
 by 
 Elizabeth Wilson 
 November 20, 2026 November 20, 2026

 Credit: Esther Quintanilla / CVJC 
 Reading Time: 4 minutes 
 Large swells of students stood in line for hours into the night to cast ballots at UC Merced on Election Day, prompting a squad of Good Samaritans to assist those who patiently waited. 
 It was the first time UC Merced has had a voting center on campus since 2018. The line snaked around the Conference Center as well as inside the building. Elections officials confirmed the last student voted at 11:30 p.m. Nov. 3.
 In years past, students had to take public transit or drive to one of the voting centers in Merced. The UC Merced campus sits about seven miles from downtown, a short distance from Lake Yosemite.
 More than 730 people cast a provisional ballot at the university vote center, the highest number of provisional ballots ever cast in the county according to Melvin Levey, Merced County registrar of voters. At least 200 people cast regular ballots at the center as well. 
 When delays were reported at UC Merced, local organizations and volunteers took action. Volunteers brought pizzas, water and drove students to other voting centers with shorter lines before the 8 p.m. closure of the polls. Despite the delays, a fervor to vote kept spirits high throughout the evening. Long lines were also reported at other college campuses including Stanislaus State, UC Santa Cruz and UC Riverside, according to Levey.

 In Merced County , 75,576 voters cast ballots, just over 55% of the county’s electorate. More than 2,000 ballots were provisional ballots – meaning people who registered to vote on Election Day. 
 The number of Merced County registered voters ages 18 through 25 was 23,456 or 17.25% of the total number of registered voters, according to a report last year from the California Secretary of State .
 Delays at UC Merced voting center  
 Delays at UC Merced were indicative of a higher volume of people and students’ interest to vote, Levey said. This year’s midterm election is set to have 20,000 more votes cast in Merced County than four years ago, he said.
 “As our university continues to grow, we look forward to working with the county to explore ways to streamline the voting experience and address challenges such as long lines in future elections,” wrote Tonantzin Oseguera, vice chancellor for student affairs and engagement in a statement to The FOCUS.
 Edgar Tello, a junior studying public health and psychology, entered and exited the line twice between classes. He returned around 7:45 p.m. and stayed in line for almost four hours, he said. It was student momentum and a desire to vote that kept him there. 
 “It’s pretty great that we had a site on campus this time, because I don’t believe we had one last year. It was pretty amazing, just because UC Merced is separate from the city, and it can be difficult to go into any other voting site in the city,” Tello said.
 Mia Carbajal, a junior studying political science at UC Merced, waited in line with her friend for three hours. Carbajal already dropped off her mail-in ballot, and she wanted to support her friend’s first-time voting. 
 “It was really inspiring to see how these students persevered through the long line and waited until midnight, knowing that they had class or midterms or assignments to turn in, just to make their vote count,” Carbajal said.
 When the line had hours-long delays, Carbajal coordinated with Sol Rivas, executive director of Valley Onward . Rivas carpooled students three times from UC Merced to other voting locations in the city. At least eight other cars helped carpool students.
 Students filled her car with chatter on voting or calls to family members. Their excitement brought Rivas to tears. She thought  of her young daughter getting the chance to vote one day.
 “They lit up my heart, and I was like, ‘OK, this is all worth it,’” Rivas said.
 Organizations collaborate for pollwatching program 
 Volunteers collaborated from multiple organizations across the San Joaquin Valley before and during Election Day.
 Movement Solidarity Among AAPI Communities (MOSAIC) received a statewide grant to partner with local organizations  to create a pollwatchers program. Coalition partners included MOVE the Valley, Faith in the Valley , Valley Onward , Community Water Center , Jakarta Movement, Communities for New California Education Fund and more.
 There were 184 pollwatchers from each of these organizations dispatched to 269 voting centers across the San Joaquin Valley, according to Mai Thao, executive director of MOVE the Valley. Those located in Merced went to UC Merced to help with the long lines.
 “From a nonpartisan perspective, it was our goal and our intention to ensure that, again, every eligible voter did vote in this election,” Thao said.
 Abdi Soltani, executive director of the ACLU of Northern California drove from the Bay Area to Merced on Election Day. When poll monitors reported long lines at UC Merced, he spent the day there. At one point, he estimated seeing 400 students in line.
 Abdi Soltani stands with a cart full of Gatorade drinks and tea to give to students during their long wait at the UC Merced voting center on Nov. 3. Photo courtesy of Abdi Soltani 
 “The drivers would pull up, and then we would ask students, ‘Does anyone want to leave to go vote, and be driven there and be brought back?’” Soltani said.
 Soltani walked the line for hours. He talked to students and handed them pizzas, water and Gatorade. He made a pact with the last student who got in line just before 8 p.m.  that he would stay until she voted. 
 “The two things that really stood out to me was one, their steadfast determination to cast their votes, and second was their patience and their respect for the election workers and for each other, and just a spirit that was serious, resolute, and so respectful,” Soltani said.
 Election results are expected to be certified by Nov. 30.
 A vehicle’s trunk is filled with pizza that was bought to give to UC Merced students during Election Day on Nov. 3. Photo courtesy of Abdi Soltani
